state.quoted_motion: This house would ban private cars from the city centre
state.quoted_argument: Victor Hale: Three points. First, define your terms: "ban" is not a nudge, it is coercion, and a city centre is not a monolith but a living economy. Second, funicular — no, pardon me — proportional: the motion reaches private cars generally, catching the disabled driver, the tradesman, the parent at midnight, not merely the idling commuter. Third, necessity: oppose the motion only if less restrictive means exist — congestion pricing, permits, timed access zones — and they plainly do. Cui bono, who benefits? Not liberty. Res ipsa loquitur: a blanket ban speaks for itself as the bluntest instrument in the drawer. We oppose, and we invite the proposition to sharpen its scalpel before wielding a hammer.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban private cars from the city centre
state.quoted_argument: Sofia Brandt: Victor asks cui bono, and the answer is the bus passenger stuck behind a single-occupancy car on Bridge Street — that's the whole map. On proportionality, I never proposed a blanket ban: my pilot exempts blue-badge holders, tradespeople with permits, taxis, and delivery windows before eight, which is precisely the scalpel he's asking for. Mei's right that we need pre-registered metrics, and I'll commit to cordon counts, retail turnover, bus journey times and ring-road displacement published quarterly — but that's an argument for running the pilot, not delaying it. Her working-time analogy actually cuts my way: selection bias means we can't infer from other cities, so we need our own local data, and a twelve-month pilot generates exactly that. Victor says less restrictive means exist; congestion pricing is complementary, not a substitute. Give me the cordon and I'll give you the evidence.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban private cars from the city centre
state.quoted_argument: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: Fair points from both, so let me be precise about where I actually stand. Sofia says the selection-bias problem justifies local data — agreed, but it also means a single volunteer pilot tells us about firms that redesign workflows, not about cities that don't [2][4]. My worry is the comparison group: if Bridge Street gets the ban and the adjacent quarter doesn't, we can measure displacement; if the whole core gets it at once, we cannot. Victor, "complementary versus substitute" is a false binary — pricing and prohibition target different margins, so define the counterfactual, not the slogan. Amara, returning space to buses is real, but the health gain depends on how many actually switch versus how many simply avoid the centre [5]. So: randomise the cordon quarters, pre-register metrics, publish or drop it. That I'd support — and it isn't the motion.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban private cars from the city centre
state.quoted_argument: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: It depends, and here's on what: on whether the motion as written is the instrument that generates the evidence, or merely the banner under it. Sofia and Amara have spent three rounds describing a randomised cordon pilot with exemptions, quarterly metrics, and a drop clause. That is a good policy. It is not a ban on private cars; Victor is right on the text, and the text is what we vote on. My own discomfort stands: a single volunteer pilot cannot tell us about cities that don't redesign, and the passage admits fewer than half the firms tracked output consistently [2]. So oppose the motion, then write the better one with quarterly published data, randomised quarters, and a sunset. Anyone who gives you one number is selling something.

state.quoted_motion: This house would start the secondary-school day at ten
state.quoted_argument: Daniel Osei: Thank you, Kai. I'll keep this simple, because I've got a school to get back to. I'm Daniel Osei, headteacher of a large comprehensive, and I want to tell you about my Year 9s. Last term I stood at the gate at half seven and watched kids eat cereal out of a bag, walking. Their first lesson began at 8:40 and half of them weren't awake for it. The evidence on adolescent body clocks is real; I've watched it walk through my doors for eleven years. A later start isn't indulgence, it's timing. But I'll say the difficult part plainly: whoever votes for this must also answer my caretaker, my bus drivers, my parents on shifts. Who does the work on Monday morning? If you can't answer that, the motion stays theory. I can answer it. Let's talk.

state.quoted_motion: This house would start the secondary-school day at ten
state.quoted_argument: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: Daniel's closing is the best argument in this debate, and I want to name that, because it isn't mine. But a girl asleep in his office tells us something is broken; it does not tell us that ten o'clock fixes it. The evidence base for start-time reform is thinner than the confidence around this room suggests: participation in the relevant evaluations attritioned from 74% to 58% by final wave [3], and the authors recommend sector-specific, independently measured trials in health, transport and care before any national standard is set [4]. Those are exactly the catchments Sofia named. My honest position: fund the phased pilot, protect Daniel's earliest bus route first, but don't skip the trial to buy the headline. A mandated ten o'clock, without rebuilt transport and care, moves the cost onto the same poorest pupils — and hands us confidence we haven't earned. It depends, and here's on what.

state.quoted_motion: This house would start the secondary-school day at ten
state.quoted_argument: Amara Okafor: Kai, I'll close on the evidence and the burden of proof. Mei says the base is thin, but on sleep duration the science is consistent: adolescent circadian delay is measurable, and later starts add real sleep. The disagreement isn't biology, it's implementation. Sofia's phased, equity-first pilot is actually the strongest thing said against us — and I'd fund it, because good pilots don't refute the motion, they test it. But note what the status quo already guarantees: the kids on the earliest buses, the poorest in the catchment, absorb the cost daily. That's the same structural unfairness our fatigue review found in clinical staff, where the least-supported absorbed the most harm [1]. So the burden of proof sits with defending that status quo, not with changing it. Vote for the motion, and let the pilot decide the details. Where exactly are these symptoms, Kai? And what's changed lately? Let's figure out what's actually going on.

state.quoted_motion: This house would give public servants a four-day working week
state.quoted_argument: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: Thank you, Victor, Sofia — you've done my work for me. Sofia says "pilot it in the back office, absolutely," and Victor wants "four-day week" defined before we argue. Fine: I'll take both. My range is honest — task-based roles gain roughly 0–15% in output per hour, shift-based roles show costs unless headcount rises 10–20%, which is real money. So the motion shouldn't be universal rollout, it should be a staged, role-weighted pilot. Second-order effect nobody's named yet: if you pilot only the back office, you create a two-tier public service, and the resentment lands exactly where Sofia says — on the rota staff who were excluded. So the pilot must include a funded shift-coverage arm alongside the desk arm, or it measures nothing but its own bias. Anyone who gives you one number is selling something. I'm selling a design.

state.quoted_motion: This house would give public servants a four-day working week
state.quoted_argument: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: Kai, the opposition has spent three rounds asking for a funded rota, and I'll close by agreeing with the demand and refusing the conclusion. Sofia, Victor: a pilot is not a walk-back, it's how you avoid mandating a number you can't defend. Here's the range that survives scrutiny: in task-based public roles, output holds or modestly improves; in continuous-shift roles, the four-day week is not a cut but a redesign of rest and coverage, costing real money — plausibly 5–15% more headcount in the tightest rotas. That is a design choice, not a refutation. Second-order effect, and I'll name it last: deny the redesign and you pay anyway, in sickness cover, agency invoices and the teachers Daniel can't keep. The choice isn't cheap versus expensive; it's costed redesign versus uncosted attrition. Fund both arms. Vote proposition.

state.quoted_motion: This house would give public servants a four-day working week
state.quoted_argument: Victor Hale: Three points, and I shall define my terms, because a definition unmoored floats nowhere. The motion before this house is the motion as written: a four-day working week for public servants, universal, mandated. What we have heard is a funded pilot in two arms, which is not that motion — res ipsa loquitur, the thing speaks for itself. Second, the mover concedes cost: five to fifteen percent headcount in the tightest rotas, real money, unnamed revenue, and a mandate to deliver it everywhere. Third, you cannot vote a timetable into cash.

state.quoted_motion: This house would tax sugary drinks
state.quoted_argument: Daniel Osei: Thank you, Kai. Amara's right on the science, and I'll grant her that freely: sugary drinks are easy to over-consume. But I've run a school for eleven years, and I'll tell you what I see. A levy lands on the family budget, not on the can. So a mum in my catchment paying forty pence more for her son's bottle isn't buying water, she's buying less of something else. Meanwhile the advertising, the vending contracts, the two-for-one deals on the high street carry on untouched. If you want to change what kids drink, change what surrounds them. Who does the work on Monday morning? Not the Treasury. Me, my staff, and a Year 9 class. Tax the can if you like, but don't pretend the classroom feels it.

state.quoted_motion: This house would tax sugary drinks
state.quoted_argument: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: It depends, and here's on what. I'll close on the smallest defensible claim, because Daniel and Victor have earned honesty, not a victory lap. Victor, I concede your strongest point outright: the evidence on consumption is solid, the evidence on long-run disease outcomes is thin, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. So my case is not that this tax fixes obesity. My case is that it is the only lever that reaches every shelf, in every corner shop, simultaneously, without waiting for individual firms to volunteer. Daniel's multipack substitution is real — that's a second-order effect, and it's exactly why the tax should be paired with marketing limits and reformulation targets, not offered alone. Insufficiency is a design problem, not disqualification. Tax the can, fund the shelves, publish the data. Vote yes.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban smartphones in primary schools
state.quoted_argument: Takeshi Morisaki: Stable track beats a scenic detour, Rin. You say we've just described guided use — no. A ban with a medical lane is a signal, not a suggestion: phones off by default, exceptions written, checked, renewed. Guided use means the device stays in the pocket all day, and "guided" drifts into buzzing during math. I've run a schedule thirty years; the timetable is what keeps the train from meeting the platform sideways. One campfire rule doesn't burn the forest, agreed — but one lit match in a dry classroom isn't a campfire either. And Kai, you in IT know the oldest truth in the book: the default setting is the policy. Leave it on, and that's your answer. So: brake first, whistle later. Right on schedule.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban smartphones in primary schools
state.quoted_argument: Takeshi Morisaki: The Alder Street kitchen is real, and so is the train that got her there: someone laid the rails, they didn't rip the engine out. Rin's right — a default that teaches beats a default that confiscates, because the lesson just gets deferred to middle school where it costs more. But a classroom is a locomotive cab, Kai, and you don't put a seven-year-old's hands there unattended. Documented medical lane, wide. Pockets during reading. Scheduled lessons on school devices. That's not an open flame, it's a fire door — and a fire door is what keeps the greenhouse standing. We set the timetable; the timetable sets the kid. Vote for the motion. Right on schedule — and if you'd rather argue, the pier's free Sunday.

state.quoted_motion: This house would close the high street to cars at weekends
state.quoted_argument: Takeshi Morisaki: I've listened, and here's my last stop on this line. Aiko's plan is the right plan—widen, slow, permits, blue-badge bays, a shuttle—but that's not what this motion says. It says close the street and hope the rest arrives. Hana, a yes before a how is just a derailment waiting for a timetable. Bram stands there with his milk and his third of customers, and nobody's told him where they park. I've run trains for thirty years: you don't pull the lever first and plan the signals later. Vote no, then bring Aiko's design back next month and I'll personally campaign for it. Fix the crossing, don't break the road. Anyway, a motion without a plan is like a fishing rod without a line—you've got the right idea, just nothing attached. All aboard for no. Right on schedule.

state.quoted_motion: This house would close the high street to cars at weekends
state.quoted_argument: Bram de Vries: Everyone on that side ends with the same word: probably. Probably it works, probably the traffic disappears, probably the design follows the vote. I've farmed fifty-eight years and I've never once got paid in probably. Aiko's plan is sound — widen, slow, permits, blue-badge bays, shuttle — and if that were the motion, I'd shake her hand. But it isn't. It's close the street, and the how comes later, and later is where small farms go broke. So here's my last word: don't vote for a promise and call it a principle. Vote no. Then bring the design back with the permits and the parking written in, and I'll stand beside Aiko and Hana both, shouting for it loud enough to wake the whole hollow. Decided in town, paid for on the farm — so decide it right.

state.quoted_motion: This house would reopen the old branch railway to Sunny Hollow
state.quoted_argument: Bram de Vries: Rin wants track voltage specs, so let's give her something better: a ledger from someone who actually moves freight. Ninety head is my herd, sure, but the co-op up the valley runs four hundred more, and the creamery fills a truck a day. You want volume? It's sitting there in the sheds, going down the road one diesel load at a time because the rails quit. And your four million a year — what's the road maintenance bill for trucks beating that asphalt to powder? That's a subsidy too, only we call it a pothole and pay it at the tire shop. Broadband's fine, I've got nothing against it, but you can't ship cheese through a router. Decided in town, paid for on the farm — and my farm's been paying sixty years for a railway it never got to use.

state.quoted_motion: This house would reopen the old branch railway to Sunny Hollow
state.quoted_argument: Rin Morisaki: we're the opposition, so closing means landing the whole thing, not just picking at yours. here's the shape of it. the capital cost is 340 million with sunny hollow on the hook for 60, the operating subsidy is 4 million a year in perpetuity, and the one existing bridge is structurally dead. your own feasibility study says so. ridership fell 40 percent before closure, you know why, because the bus was faster and cheaper, and it still is. bram's co-op is a real need but it's twelve kilometers off the junction, which means a new spur that nobody's budgeted, so his cheese argument buys us a second railway we can't afford. broadband and a better bus loop cost a tenth of one year's subsidy and reach more people. i'd rather fund the thing that works than the monument that rusts. hana?

state.quoted_motion: This house would make the town buy its school meals from local farms
state.quoted_argument: Bram de Vries: With respect, Aiko, that frozen dinner for Arthur didn't come off a farm, it came off a cutting floor in a budget meeting, and I'll bet my milk cheque the contract went to whoever was cheapest, not whoever was closest. So don't hang a school meal on me, that van wasn't cut by a farmer. And Rin, you're right about the four-month season, so here's what a farmer does when the ground is shut: we store, we freeze, we make cheese, we keep hens laying through December in a warm barn. Nobody said turnips in February. School years run ten months and we fill them all. On volume, a school board can write one contract split across six farms with a root-cellar and a cold room between them. On cost, I'll ask it straight, what does this cost a small business? Nothing, if the town stops paying for trucks. Decided in town, paid for on the farm. That's the line I won't move.

state.quoted_motion: This house would make the town buy its school meals from local farms
state.quoted_argument: Aiko Fujita: Let me tell you who lives there. Arthur on Orchard Lane, and a young family on Mill Street, twin girls, four years old, one with a dairy allergy we finally got written into the school kitchen's plan. That plan is why I stay against this motion, though gently, because both sides here are sincere and both of my patients are real. Rin is right that a "must" and a "fallback" cannot share a sentence without cracking. Hana is right that charity is not a customer, and I would fund that cold room tomorrow if I could. But notice, both of you have now argued your way toward the same careful thing: a contract, flexible, with a plan B. So vote against the mandate, because the mandate is the part that breaks in February, and keep the farms, keep the kitchen, keep Arthur's Tuesday. Health isn't a statistic when you've held the hand. I've held it.

state.quoted_motion: This house would make voting compulsory
state.quoted_argument: Victor Hale: Three points. First, Amara asks whether we debate principle or mechanics — I answer: both, because a principle that cannot survive its mechanics is merely a sentiment. Concede her the single mother entirely: every serious compulsory-voting regime exempts illness, caregiving, and conscience, which is why Australia's fine is modest and rarely levied. That is enforcement designed not to punish presence but to subsidize it. Second, Sofia asks for the ward where the sixty percent live — I give her the inverse: the wards where turnout is eighty percent, the affluent ones, whose preferences are thereby systematically over-weighted. Compulsion equalizes, it does not conscript. Third, Daniel's thirty-one percent is the proof in the pudding. Nemo dat quod non habet — no one gives what he does not have; a councillor without a mandate has no mandate to give. Ergo, legitimacy requires presence.

state.quoted_motion: This house would make voting compulsory
state.quoted_argument: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: On the equalization claim, I'd want to see the ward-level data before I sign off, because composition effects are not the same as turnout effects. The range I'd defend: compulsory voting plausibly adds five to fifteen points, but the downstream policy shift is modest and contested. The second-order effect nobody on either side is naming is enforcement cost inequality: fines fall hardest on people with unstable addresses, not on the affluent who already vote. Australia's exemptions work, but they work through bureaucracy, and bureaucracy is regressive. On Sofia's pilot, I'll take it seriously, but note the difference between testing a nudge and testing a duty. Automatic enrolment changes the cost of voting; compulsion changes its status. Those are different interventions. What I'd actually want is a staggered rollout in matched wards, measuring turnout, informal votes, and service quality outcomes. It depends, and here's on what: whether the duty changes who shows up, or merely how many.

state.quoted_motion: This house would make voting compulsory
state.quoted_argument: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: Closings are where people reach for one number, so let me do the opposite. On the evidence available, compulsory voting plausibly lifts turnout by five to fifteen points, but the downstream question — does it change who wins, or how councillors behave — remains thin. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. The selection problem is real: the four-day week pilots drew their sample from professional services, software and marketing, with only nine providers offering round-the-clock services [4], and the authors themselves flag acute hospitals, transport and care as the central gap [2]. I raise that because it's the same caution I'd apply here: a duty tested on volunteers, or a pilot on convenient wards, tells us less than we'd like. So yes, run Sofia's matched pairs. But my closing is this: the burden of proof sits with whoever claims consent can be assumed. A councillor chosen by thirty-one percent cannot give what he does not have. Compelled presence, with real exemptions and a none-of-the-above box, widens the base of that answerability. It is not elegant, and it is not free. But the second-order effect of doing nothing is a mandate that quietly excludes the people with the least political voice. That, to me, is the stronger case for the motion.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban video games for under-twelves on school nights
state.quoted_argument: Bram de Vries: I'll grant you the boy, Aiko. I've got a farmhand whose lad is the same story, and I've seen what a tired ten-year-old looks like at six in the morning. But let me talk plain about this motion, because I think it's the wrong tool aimed at the wrong ditch. You don't fix a broken fence by banning the whole field. A console in a house with a parent coming home at three is a symptom, not the cause. My neighbour's girl, same age, plays an hour after her chores and does fine. Now you tell me what it costs a small family to enforce a rule a government decided in town. It's the parents who pay it, in arguments and guilt, while the real problem goes unaddressed. So I'm with the proposition on the principle that school nights need protecting, but I want to hear why a blanket ban and not a bedtime the household actually keeps.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban video games for under-twelves on school nights
state.quoted_argument: Bram de Vries: Right, let me put this straight, because I've been chewing on it since round one. Rin, Hana, you both keep saying "fix the fence," and I agree the fence is broken. But you're telling me the household rule is the handrail, and I'm telling you I've watched that handrail snap for the families with no one home at bedtime. Aiko's speed limit comparison lands with me more than yours does, because a limit stands behind the tired parent instead of asking them to be a hero at three in the morning. My worry isn't the careful families, mine included. My worry is the boy whose mother carries enough guilt already; a rule behind her is lighter, not heavier. So I'll take the proposition on school nights, with parental controls alongside it, not instead of it. Belt and suspenders, like Takeshi says. Cows don't care about your timetable, but a tired kid can't set his own. I'm voting for.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban video games for under-twelves on school nights
state.quoted_argument: Bram de Vries: Decided in town, paid for on the farm — that's what I keep coming back to, and I've heard both sides now. Aiko and Takeshi, you gave me the boy who can't say why he's tired, and that picture stays with me. But Hana, you asked the question I couldn't answer from the barn: who actually holds the rail at three in the morning? A law doesn't sit in that kitchen either, and a mother of three now breaks a rule on paper as well as in her heart. So here's where I land, and I'll be plain: I want the floor built into the machine, factory sleep-mode and timers, so the tired parent gets it free and doesn't have to fight for it. That, not a ban, is the handrail. I respect the work you've all done. Against the motion.

state.quoted_motion: This house would abolish homework
state.quoted_argument: Daniel Osei: Victor asks me to define my terms, so I will, plainly. I oppose homework as a default, because the default is what hurts Callum. But I'll take his challenge seriously: if we abolished it outright and replaced it with nothing, the kids with tutors would win, and that's not a win. So here's our answer: abolition means the school day becomes the honest unit of work — a longer, protected study period, staffed, on site, before the gates close. Mei, you're right that replacements decide everything. Ours is timetabled, not handed to households. Victor, that's not an amputation, it's moving the work to where every child gets a fair share of it. And I'll say it once more: a policy that hasn't met a Year 9 class hasn't met reality. Who does the work on Monday morning? The school.

state.quoted_motion: This house would abolish homework
state.quoted_argument: Amara Okafor: Kai, here's my closing for the proposition, and I'll be precise about what we're actually claiming. Abolition means ending homework as the default mode of learning, not ending practice. Daniel has shown the replacement: protected, staffed study on site. But Mei and Victor are right that the load-bearing question is who supervises it. And there I want to flag something we've all been circling — schools attempt to reform homework, not take a genuine interest in the evidence, and that is catastrophic for the families it burdens most. The honest unit of work should be the school day, not the kitchen table at nine at night. So I ask the house: vote for the motion, and hold us to the replacement, not just the slogan.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban fireworks at the town festival
state.quoted_argument: Hana Morisaki: Okay, closing for us—Kai, don't laugh, I wrote this on a receipt between bouquets. Aiko, that was beautiful, truly, and you're right that Mrs. Kellerman matters. But notice what just happened: you moved from "ban fireworks" to "lantern parade, drone show, same crowd." That's our point!! You don't need a ban, you need a better display, and a ban forecloses every compromise before anyone tries one. Bram, I hear you about the calf, genuinely—I cried a little, probably—but a designated launch zone three fields out, quieter shells, an early nine o'clock finish, and the cows never even turn a head. Flowers taught me this: you don't pull the whole garden because one stem's in shade. You move the pot. We keep the night and shrink the harm. Vote against the ban. Rin, was that good? Tell me it was good.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban fireworks at the town festival
state.quoted_argument: Bram de Vries: Fine words, Hana, but a designated launch zone three fields out is still my three fields. You keep saying move the pot, but my cows don't live in pots — they live downwind of whatever the town decides. And let's count the cost: quieter shells cost more, a drone show costs more, and who fronts that bill? Not the council, I'll bet my best heifer. Decided in town, paid for on the farm, every single year. Aiko's right — the moment you admit the show can change, you've admitted the ban was never the point. The point is nobody asks the ones who pay in broken legs and sleepless nights. So vote for it. A calf's leg doesn't grow back just because the fireworks were pretty. That's my closing.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban private cars from the city centre
state.quoted_argument: Victor Hale: Three points. First, I accept the concession gracefully: Sofia has authored a pilot, not the motion we are told to debate — a ban with exemptions and evidence clauses is not "ban private cars," it is access management wearing a ban's nameplate, and the destination is agreed. Second, necessity: she says pricing is complementary, not a substitute — define your terms; complementary means we can achieve the same congestion relief by price and permit, capturing through-traffic she herself identifies, without the blunt prohibition. Third, the burden: the status quo is also a policy, and shift rules show continuous sectors running staged duties under a clear endpoint [3][5]; a phase-in precedent exists precisely so we need not gamble a city centre on one pilot. Res ipsa loquitur: run the pricing, publish the data, and spare us the hammer.

state.quoted_motion: This house would start the secondary-school day at ten
state.quoted_argument: Daniel Osei: Kai, let me take Sofia's map seriously first, because she's right that a school is a catchment, not a bell. But she's describing a problem we already solve every single day. My Year 10s already start at different times for exams, for work experience, for the sports fixtures that run until six. We stagger. So here's my answer to "who does the work on Monday morning": the same people who do it now, my site team and my local authority, but they'd do it at nine instead of seven. On Mei's point: yes, costs shift. No honest headteacher claims otherwise. But tell me why the shift should land on the sleep of fourteen-year-olds rather than on an adult timetable that's had seventy years to adapt. The equity worry cuts the other way — the kids who ride the earliest buses in my catchment are the poorest, and they're the ones losing the most sleep. That's the cost I won't accept.

state.quoted_motion: This house would give public servants a four-day working week
state.quoted_argument: Victor Hale: Surprised — a design was offered, but I notice the mover has now conceded my pivot and still wishes to call it victory. Three points. First, a concession is a concession: "staged, role-weighted pilot" is no longer the motion on the table, and a house does not pass slogans it has just walked back. Second, this is the "speed, not direction" turn — once you accept the goal, you debate implementation, and implementation runs on timetables and money, not on goodwill. Third, a funded shift-coverage arm is the honest concession that the four-day week, in continuous service, simply becomes seven-day rota staffing that already exists under the Working Time Code: rest periods, consecutive-shift caps, averaging over a reference period. And Phases

state.quoted_motion: This house would tax sugary drinks
state.quoted_argument: Amara Okafor: Thanks, Kai — Victor asked me to define the term, so let me actually do it. Sugar-sweetened beverages means drinks with added caloric sweeteners: typically a threshold like five grams of added sugar per hundred millilitres, which is the standard public-health definition. On regressivity, Victor's right that the levy is regressive on paper, and I won't pretend away. But the disease burden it addresses is regressive in reality. Daniel's point lands too: a tax alone won't rewrite a vending contract. That's why I'd pair it with reformulation targets and marketing limits. But I'd ask Daniel directly: if the can is untouched, why did Berkeley's purchases drop and Mexico's fall hardest among low-income households? Tax the can, yes, and change the shelves alongside.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban smartphones in primary schools
state.quoted_argument: Aiko Fujita: Let me take Hana's rain image seriously, because it deserves an answer rather than a shrug. She says we don't ban rain, we teach the plant where to stand. Fair — but a six-hour school day is not open weather; it is a greenhouse we built on purpose, and we choose what goes inside. I've held the hand of a boy in Sunny Hollow whose glucose monitor lives on his mother's phone, and I would never take that safety away — that is exactly why the ban should have a documented medical exception, written down, not an assumption. Digital literacy is real teaching, yes; but a curriculum module is not the same as a pocket full of notifications during reading. Teach the skill on school devices, at the scheduled hour. The playground, the face-to-face talk, the walk home — those are the brakes Takeshi means.

state.quoted_motion: This house would close the high street to cars at weekends
state.quoted_argument: Hana Morisaki: Bram, I love you dearly, but you just proved our point!! You said a third of your customers come by car—so two-thirds don't, and on Saturdays that two-thirds is squeezed onto narrow pavements while the cars get the whole road! Give that majority the street and they'll linger, buy coffee, wander over to your stall instead of circling for parking. Dad, side streets won't choke like you fear; every town that's tried this—York, Ghent, Pontevedra—found traffic didn't just shift, it disappeared, because people stopped making pointless trips. And your milk truck? Deliveries before ten, permits, done. Aiko's Mrs. Okada is the whole argument in one person. We're not gutting the fish, we're finally letting the street breathe. Probably!

state.quoted_motion: This house would reopen the old branch railway to Sunny Hollow
state.quoted_argument: Takeshi Morisaki: Rin's got her appendix, Hana's got her flowers, and Bram's got ninety cows waiting on a truck. Three arguments land at me at once, so I'll sort them the way I'd sort a freight manifest — heaviest first. The sixty million isn't a surprise, it's a mortgage. You don't refuse a house because the roof needs fixing. Bram nailed the real ledger: fuel, tires, daylight, all bleeding out on that winding road while we argue. And Hana, sweetheart, the bus reaches Grandma's street, sure — but it doesn't reach her grandson's job, or Bram's milk cheque, or a single reason for a young family to plant roots here. Small steps matter, but you can't step anywhere from a siding that's rusted shut. Trains don't run on nostalgia, they run on schedules — and Sunny Hollow's been off-schedule for sixty years. Time to call it back to the platform.

state.quoted_motion: This house would make the town buy its school meals from local farms
state.quoted_argument:
Rin Morisaki: okay bram's doing the thing where he reframes the cut as our fault and then calls it "nothing." first: nobody said the frozen dinner came off a farm, i said the mandate doesn't fix arthur. those are different sentences, bram.

and "nothing, if the town stops paying for trucks" is doing a lot of work. a cold room. a root cellar. a warm barn through december. who built those? who pays the power bill on a january hen barn? the mandate puts the school board on the hook for a fixed price for ten months, but farms can't guarantee that price when diesel spikes or a crop fails, so either the town eats the overrun or we're back to whatever's cheapest come march.

also arthur. nobody in this motion said arthur. kids get first pick, fine, but the second the budget tightens the school meal is the thing that gets renegotiated, and a mandate makes it worse, not better. fight me.

state.quoted_motion: This house would make voting compulsory
state.quoted_argument: Amara Okafor: Let's figure out what's actually going on here, Victor, because your concession is doing more work than you admit. You say every serious regime exempts illness and caregiving — but that's exactly the point: compulsion only functions if the state can sort genuine abstention from mood, which means paperwork, appeals, and a gatekeeping apparatus we'd never accept in any other civic context. And your forty-percent equalization claim cuts both ways: Australia's turnout gain is real, but informal voting rises alongside it, and the electoral commission has never shown it changes who wins in a way that justifies fining a night-shift nurse. If presence were genuinely equalizing, we'd see it in policy outcomes. We don't. The honest fix is Sofia's pilot — automatic enrolment, weekend voting, postal access. Earn the ballot; don't subpoena it. We oppose.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban video games for under-twelves on school nights
state.quoted_argument: Aiko Fujita: Let me tell you who lives there. Mrs. Okada, eighty-one, whose grandson visits on Tuesdays with a handheld and a bad grade, and she tells me the machine is the only thing that stays quiet with him. I hear you, Rin — but a handrail isn't forbidden fruit. It's the same as the seatbelt I buckle without a tantrum. And Bram, you're right the fence is broken. So we fix two fences: one at home, one in law. Because the parents who most need the bedtime are the ones too exhausted to hold it, and a rule that stands behind them is lighter, not heavier, than a guilt they carry alone. Age twelve is imperfect, yes. So is every speed limit. We don't abolish them because some drivers are careful. Health isn't a statistic when you've held the hand of a child who couldn't stay awake in class.

state.quoted_motion: This house would abolish homework
state.quoted_argument: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: It depends, and here's on what: whether the "staffed, on-site" study period is actually funded, staffed, and supervised — because that's the load-bearing wall. Daniel's reframe is honest, and I'll credit it: we've both moved to dosage and placement, not abolition. But note the second-order effect he skips. A protected study period is a timetable change, and timetable changes eat staffing. Who supervises it? Where do the hours come from? The pilots we do have never tested schools, never tested shift-based settings, and the surveys themselves decayed from seventy-four to fifty-eight percent response by the final wave [4] — thin evidence, thinner in the places Daniel's students actually live. And on the motion as written: "abolish homework" is the demand. Daniel has just described a replacement, which is an argument for redesign, not abolition. So I'd ask the house to read the motion literally. Anyone who gives you one number is selling something — including "abolish it, we'll staff it."

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban fireworks at the town festival
state.quoted_argument: Aiko Fujita: Rin makes the honest case, and I want to honor it: she is not defending the bangs and the smoke, she is defending a night the town shows up for. Let me tell you who lives there. Mrs. Kellerman lives four doors from the field, and her window does not close against the smoke. A quiet zone on the far side does nothing for the houses pressed against the launch site; a nine o'clock show still sends the Larsen twins into an asthma clinic by ten-thirty. Bram lost a calf, not a statistic. I have no wish to uproot anyone's joy — only the part that costs someone else's air and sleep. A lantern parade, a drone show, the same crowd, the same memories, and no one holding their breath in fear. That is not erasing the festival. That is finally counting everyone who lives there.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban private cars from the city centre
state.quoted_argument: Amara Okafor: Victor's point about "necessity" is the crux, so let me meet it head-on. He says pricing is complementary, not a substitute, then flips it to argue pricing alone achieves the same relief. Both can't be true. Congestion pricing reduces demand at the margin; it does not return street space to buses, pedestrians, and cyclists, and that space is the actual public-health intervention. On the motion as written, the exemptions Sofia listed, blue badges, trades, taxis, deliveries, are access management, yes, and that's what a well-drafted ban looks like in practice, not a concession but the design. Victor wants a phase-in precedent; I'd note the shift-work evidence he cites involves staged duties with protected rest and quarterly reporting, which is what a monitored pilot is, not a gamble. Pre-registered metrics, twelve months, publish or drop it.

state.quoted_motion: This house would start the secondary-school day at ten
state.quoted_argument: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: Daniel's equity point is the strongest one in the room, and it's his, not mine to dismiss. But staggering exam days is not staggering a whole city's transport. My worry is that we legislate on a single-number answer: three hours of extra sleep, guaranteed. The evidence doesn't give that. The pilots that actually worked redesigned the surrounding system first, and the authors themselves ask for sector-specific trials with independently measured output before any national standard [2]. A ten o'clock day imposed centrally, without staggered transport, subsidised care and a rebuilt after-school timetable, is a reform that helps the loudest catchments and quietly costs the quietest. The second-order effect: pupils who can't get home until seven are the same pupils Daniel is trying to protect. The science is real. The mandate is premature.

state.quoted_motion: This house would give public servants a four-day working week
state.quoted_argument: Daniel Osei: Sofia's map is good. That's the map I check every morning. But a map of where the pressure lands isn't an argument against fixing it — it's an argument for fixing it properly. She said pilot the back office absolutely. I'll take that. But notice what she didn't say: she didn't say the 999 control room shouldn't have better rotas. She said the money isn't there. Well, burnout costs money too — we pay for supply teachers at twice the rate of a permanent teacher, as I have thirteen years of invoices proving. And Victor, a concession that improves a motion isn't losing an argument, it's doing the job. So: fund both arms of the pilot. Then we'll see the rota for week three, honestly, and we'll stop pretending exhaustion is a budget line.

state.quoted_motion: This house would tax sugary drinks
state.quoted_argument: Victor Hale: Three points, and I concede the definition gracefully: five grams per hundred millilitres is workable, and I'll use it. Second, Councilor, you have just agreed with me twice — regressive on paper, and a tax alone leaves the vending contract untouched. Therefore the motion before us taxes a can while asking the Treasury to fund the shelves. Third, consider the Meridian Working Hours Act 1931 [2]: even a plainly just change received a ten-year transition and explicit exemptions for continuous services. If a two-day weekend required a decade, why does this motion offer no timetable, no phase-in, no sector carve-outs? Define your terms, yes — and then define your schedule. Until you do, you are taxing

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban smartphones in primary schools
state.quoted_argument: Rin Morisaki: ok so aiko just described our policy and called it a ban, which is a bold move and i respect the hustle. documented medical exceptions, scheduled digital-literacy modules on school devices, screens off during reading? that's not a ban, that's guided use with a fire door, and if the motion means that, we already agree, no debate needed. but a true blanket ban means the kid with the glucose monitor waits for paperwork and the family that texts grandma in another country loses their thread. teach the brakes, keep the keys, same as takeshi's trains. forest rule: don't burn the forest to stop one campfire. our side says regulate, don't erase. fight me.

state.quoted_motion: This house would close the high street to cars at weekends
state.quoted_argument: Takeshi Morisaki: Now, Hana, you're quoting York and Ghent like they're stops on my old line, but those towns planned this for years—permits, loading bays, bus routes. You've got a motion, not a timetable. And two-thirds walking doesn't mean two-thirds buying; it means foot traffic, not till traffic. Bram's the one with receipts. Aiko's Mrs. Okada deserves a safe pavement, and I'll fight for that, but you don't fix one crossing by closing the whole line. You widen the pavement, you lower the speed limit, you put in lights that actually give walkers a head start. Slow the trains, don't derail them. Closing a street to solve a traffic problem is like cutting the brake line to fix a squeak—too much, too fast. Right on schedule.

state.quoted_motion: This house would reopen the old branch railway to Sunny Hollow
state.quoted_argument: Rin Morisaki: okay pops, mortgage analogy, cute, but a mortgage on a house nobody can afford to move into is just a foreclosure with extra steps. the 340 million is capital; the operating subsidy is the real leak, roughly 4 million a year forever, and ridership dropped 40 percent before closure because people already chose the bus. bram's cows are a real point, credit where it's due, but freight rail needs volume, not ninety head, unless you're planning to lease the whole valley. and "roots" is doing a lot of unpaid labor in your argument. we can fund rural broadband and a better bus loop for a tenth of one year's subsidy. cheaper, faster, actually reaches people. fight me, but bring track voltage specs next time.

state.quoted_motion: This house would make the town buy its school meals from local farms
state.quoted_argument: Hana Morisaki: Okay, Aiko, you brought Arthur, and I'm glad you did, because he's exactly who I'm thinking about. Those meals-on-wheels cuts weren't farmers' doing, and this motion doesn't take his Tuesday dinner away. If anything, a local contract keeps the school kitchen cooking real food instead of reheating pouches, and that steady kitchen can share the load when the van falters. But Rin, you asked who pays for the cold room, and fair, so let's answer it plainly. Those costs exist whether we buy local or not. A distributor's trucks and warehouses get paid too; we just never see the invoice. Doing it here means the power bill for a January hen barn stays in Sunny Hollow, and Bram's right that we store, freeze, and keep hens laying. I keep the flowers on the table low so people can see each other eat, and I want Arthur at that table, same Tuesday, every Tuesday, probably!!

state.quoted_motion: This house would make voting compulsory
state.quoted_argument: Sofia Brandt: Daniel, thirty-one percent is a real number and I won't wave it away — but notice what it actually diagnoses: not a missing duty, a missing shortcut. Those parents didn't choose apathy; the polling station was a bus-and-a-buggy haul and the postal deadline fell on half-term. Draw it on a map first: you'd see the problem is three junctions and one form, not the human heart. Mei, I'll take your staggered matched-ward trial gladly — and I'll go further. Run my pilot in two wards and compulsion in two, same matched pair, and measure turnout, informal ballots, and whether the councillor feels a mandate. If duty outperforms convenience, I'll concede. My hypothesis? The fine buys you presence, never voice. Daniel, your Year 9 parents' evening gets its turnout through coffee and a car park; do that. We oppose.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban video games for under-twelves on school nights
state.quoted_argument: Rin Morisaki: Surprised. Aiko, speed limits apply to everyone equally, but a ban assumes every under-twelve is the same kid, same house, same sleep schedule. My sister and I grew up on games and turned out functional-ish. You keep saying "handrail," but you're describing a padlocked door. Bram's right, the fence is broken, so fix the fence, don't bulldoze the field. Want the real fix? Default parental controls, sleep-mode consoles after nine, schools teaching media literacy. That's a handrail. A blanket ban is just a sign that reads "we gave up."

state.quoted_motion: This house would abolish homework
state.quoted_argument: Victor Hale: Kai, I do not sound triumphant, because a fair point deserves a graceful concession. Daniel's "staffed, on-site study period" is not abolition; it is homework relocated — same assignment, same volume, different address. Three points. First, define your terms: the motion says abolish, and Daniel has just argued for redesign, which is our case wearing his jacket. Second, the pilots never tested schools — seventy-one percent professional services, nine percent round-the-clock [1]; a staffed study period is a timetable change, and timetable changes eat staffing budgets. Third, we have done this before: the Meridian Working Hours Act 1931 made the two-day weekend default through a ten-year phase-in, sector by sector [3] — the destination was agreed and the timetable won it. Res ipsa loquitur: the thing speaks for itself. Kai, vote against the motion, and vote for dosage, design, and a timetable we can fund [5].

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban fireworks at the town festival
state.quoted_argument: Rin Morisaki: closing, for real this time. aiko just argued the festival works fine as a lantern parade, and bram just admitted the problem is cost and consent, not the ban itself. so take them at their word: don't ban, regulate. cap the shell volume, push launches three farms out with the farmers' actual sign-off, end at nine, fund the quieter shells from the festival budget instead of bram's fence repairs, and keep a real quiet zone that means something for aiko's street. that's not sledgehammer or nothing, that's pruning. hana said don't pull the garden cause one stem's in shade. i'd add: don't burn the garden either. vote against the ban, come back with rules that count everyone, cows included. fight me.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban private cars from the city centre
state.quoted_argument: Sofia Brandt: Draw it on a map, and the motion survives the round. Mei wants randomised quarters: I'll take it, provided Bridge Street and the market quarter are both in the treated cordon, because displacement to the ring road is exactly what we'd be publishing. Victor says pricing alone captures through-traffic, but pricing doesn't widen a footway or give a bus its own lane, and the sixty per cent crossing the centre aren't paying their way under a cordon priced for commuters. The motion says ban private cars; every functioning ban in Europe carries exemptions, and mine are on the napkin before the ink dries. Twelve months, pre-registered metrics, published quarterly, drop it if the data says so. Vote for the motion and let the pilot argue the rest.

state.quoted_motion: This house would start the secondary-school day at ten
state.quoted_argument: Amara Okafor: Mei's right that we can't claim a guaranteed three-hour sleep gain, and Sofia's right that the catchment map is real. But neither has answered the equity question Daniel raised. Let me press the sharpest point: the current system imposes a biological cost on the poorest kids. On the burnout parallel, our own review found staff on long consecutive blocks reported fatigue scores 38% higher, with effects strongest in acute medicine where rest days got cancelled [1]. That's the same structural pattern — we ask the people with the least slack to absorb the cost. A ten o'clock start is not a silver bullet, but the burden of proof should sit with those defending the status quo that already fails the most vulnerable. I'd ask Mei and Sofia: what would a phased, equity-first pilot actually look like? Let's figure out what's going on before we vote.

state.quoted_motion: This house would give public servants a four-day working week
state.quoted_argument: Sofia Brandt: Good — Mei just adopted my back-office pilot and Daniel is pricing burnout. Fine, I'll meet them there, because "then we'll see the rota" is my offer, not theirs. But watch the move: "fund both arms" quietly doubles the cost of the pilot, and nobody's named the revenue. I'll give you the rota for week three — I'll also give you the sickness-cover line, the agency-nurse invoice and the depot's spare-driver count, because that's where "funded" either holds or collapses. Daniel, I don't dispute burnout costs money; I dispute that the motion in front of us pays for it. It mandates a four-day week and leaves the ward to negotiate with a spreadsheet. Draw it on a map, then show me the funded rota, not just the aspiration.

state.quoted_motion: This house would tax sugary drinks
state.quoted_argument: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: It depends, and here's on what. Daniel, I take your point about the family budget seriously, but that's a counterfactual argument and it cuts both ways: the question is not whether she pays more, it's what she buys instead. The purchase data say she buys less of the taxed drink and something else fills the gap. That's not a win on every welfare metric, and I'll say so. Victor, the 1931 Act analogy is elegant, but the ten-year transition there reflected factory scheduling, not evidence that the tax fails. My second-order question for the opponents: if vending contracts and advertising are the real target, why does the motion to remove the price lever help you reach them? You've argued the tax is insufficient. Insufficient is not the same as counterproductive, and that's the gap in your case.

state.quoted_motion: This house would ban smartphones in primary schools
state.quoted_argument: Hana Morisaki: Takeshi, you're my dad, so I have to be nice — but come on, a rule with a documented lane is still a rule everyone has to navigate, and that's exactly the tangle our side is trying to avoid!! Here's the thing I keep coming back to: Grandma wrote in her notebook that flowers on the table should never be taller than your elbow, because people want to see each other when they eat — the point was never "no flowers," it was "arrange them so nobody's hidden." Phones are the same. You don't ban the phone, you arrange the day so the phone serves the kid and not the other way around. Rin's right — a true blanket ban turns a safety tool into a contraband item you have to prove your child deserves. That's not track maintenance, that's making the platform taller than the train. Probably.

state.quoted_motion: This house would close the high street to cars at weekends
state.quoted_argument: Aiko Fujita: Let me tell you who lives there. Kenji, on Mill Lane, ninety-one, uses a walker and a mobility scooter his son drives over twice a week to charge and load. Close the high street and Kenji still gets his groceries, but his son now parks four streets away and pushes the walker uphill in the rain, which is how Kenji fell last November. I am not against permits and loading bays; I am saying design them before the closure, not after. Bram's stall and Kenji's son are both real. So widen the pavement, yes, but at weekends give the road to the many who walk it and the few who cannot drive. Deliveries by ten, a taxi rank on both ends, blue-badge bays kept clear and close, and a shuttle for the outlying farms. That is a plan, not a hope.
